exercise_group.instruction: In Exercises 27–34, $$A$$ and $$B$$ are $$n \times n$$ matrices. Mark each statement True or False (T/F). Justify each answer.

problem.paragraph: (T/F) A row replacement operation does not affect the determinant of a matrix.
(T/F) If $$\det A$$ is zero, then two rows or two columns are the same, or a row or a column is zero.
(T/F) If the columns of $$A$$ are linearly dependent, then $$\det A = 0$$ .
(T/F) The determinant of $$A$$ is the product of the diagonal entries in $$A$$ .
(T/F) If three row interchanges are made in succession, then the new determinant equals the old determinant.

(T/F) The determinant of $$A$$ is the product of the pivots in any echelon form $$U$$ of $$A$$ , multiplied by $$( - 1)^{r}$$ , where $$r$$ is the number of row interchanges made during row reduction from $$A$$ to $$U$$ .
(T/F) $$\text{det(} A + B) = \text{det} A + \text{det} B$$ .
(T/F) $$\text{det} A^{- 1} = ( - 1 \text{)det} A$$ .
Compute $$\det B^{4}$$ , where $$B = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rrr} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ .
Use Theorem 3 (but not Theorem 4) to show that if two rows of a square matrix $$A$$ are equal, then $$\text{det} A = 0$$ . The same is true for two columns. Why?

exercise_group.instruction: In Exercises 37–42, mention an appropriate theorem in your explanation.

problem.paragraph: Show that if $$A$$ is invertible, then $$\text{det} A^{-1} = \frac{1}{ \text{det} A}$$ .
Suppose that $$A$$ is a square matrix such that $$\det A^{3} = 0$$ . Explain why $$A$$ cannot be invertible.
Let $$A$$ and $$B$$ be square matrices. Show that even though $$AB$$ and $$BA$$ may not be equal, it is always true that $$\text{det} AB = \text{det} BA$$ .
Let $$A$$ and $$P$$ be square matrices, with $$P$$ invertible. Show that $$\text{det(} PAP^{- 1}) = \text{det} A$$ .
Let $$U$$ be a square matrix such that $$U^{T}U = I$$ . Show that $$\text{det} U = \pm 1$$ .
Find a formula for $$\det (rA)$$ when $$A$$ is an $$n \times n$$ matrix.

exercise_group.instruction: Verify that $$\det AB = \text{(det} A \text{)(det} B)$$ for the matrices in Exercises 43 and 44. (Do not use Theorem 6.)

Let $$A = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ and $$B = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} a & b \\ c & d \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . Show that $$\text{det(} A + B) = \text{det} A + \text{det} B$$ if and only if $$a + d = 0$$ .
Note, however, that $$A$$ is not the same as $$B + C$$ .

Right-multiplication by an elementary matrix $$E$$ affects the columns of $$A$$ in the same way that left-multiplication affects the rows. Use Theorems 5 and 3 and the obvious fact that $$E^{T}$$ is another elementary matrix to show that $$\det A E = \left(\det E\right) \left(\det A\right)$$
Do not use Theorem 6.
Suppose $$A$$ is an $$n \times n$$ matrix and a computer suggests that $$\det A = 5$$ and $$\text{det(} A^{- 1}) = 1$$ . Should you trust these answers? Why or why not?
Suppose $$A$$ and $$B$$ are $$n \times n$$ matrices and a computer suggests that $$\det A = 5$$ , $$\det B = 2$$ and $$\det AB = 7$$ . Should you trust these answers? Why or why not?

[T] Compute $$\det A^{T}A$$ and $$\text{det} AA^{T}$$ for several random $$4 \times 5$$ matrices and several random $$5 \times 6$$ matrices. What can you say about $$A^{T}A$$ and $$AA^{T}$$ when $$A$$ has more columns than rows?

Compute the determinants of $$A$$ , $$10A$$ , and $$0.1A$$ . In contrast, compute the condition numbers of these matrices. Repeat these calculations when $$A$$ is the $$4 \times 4$$ identity matrix. Discuss your results.

Recall that $$\det I = 1$$ . By Theorem 6, $$\det (AA) = (\det A)(\det A)$$ . Putting these two observations together results in $$1 = \det I = \det A^{2} = \det ( A A ) = (\det A )(\det A ) = \left(\left(\right. \det A \left.\right)\right)^{2}$$
Taking the square root of both sides establishes that $$\text{det} A = \pm 1$$ .
